rv.q: In Baker’s brilliant The Antipodes (given its UK premiere at the National Theatre), the hunt for plot turns into a quest. Her characters sit around a vast, empty table, trying to dream up an original yarn.
‘The Antipodes’ – which has its UK premiere in a production co-directed by Baker herself and designer Chloe Lamford – is utterly, gloriously out there and will doubtless horrify some people.
Its disquieting mood lingers long, long after its abrupt snap ending.
Baker’s play falls apart only when the characters are left to their own devices and when it seeks to make general statements.
Annie Baker is a contemplative and challenging playwright who gives viewers an opportunity to explore the minutiae of life in great detail.
I was as gripped as I was frequently perplexed.
This is an ineffectual production of a limp idea.
It’s still Baker though who pushes dangerously at just what theatre is.
On the surface The Antipodes seems to be a satire on corporate brainstorming, but why does Sandy slowly retreat from the group and quite what is wrong with his wife Rachel?

cn.t: Baker's enigmatic meditation on storytelling divides critics: some find it gloriously surreal and fascinating, while others feel it runs out of narrative steam despite intriguing premises and strong performances.
